thesisQuality.basis: Approximately 40,000 U.S. towers and independent 23% year-over-year mobile traffic growth support durable demand, offset by company-specific churn.

financialOperatingMomentum.basis: More than $7B debt reduction improved resilience while 2026 site-rental guidance remains churn-pressured.

marketValuationOpportunity.basis: Sep. 30 market data show $66.65 close, $28.36B market cap, $50.72B EV, 16.82x price/FFO and 6.38% yield; valuation reset offers headroom but leverage and growth uncertainty remain.

catalystScore.basis: Post-divestiture cost/debt actions and the next operating update can clarify normalized tower growth, but catalyst realization remains execution-dependent.

governancePower.basis: Management executed the divestiture, debt reduction and $1B repurchases, while post-sale growth durability remains unproven.

alignment2036.basis: Macro towers support durable connectivity needs and independent data show strong North American traffic/5G adoption, though carrier spend can shift architectures.

crossDivisionLeverage.basis: The divestiture created a pure-play U.S. tower company, reducing independent demand engines and increasing dependence on one infrastructure class and carrier set.

bottleneckControl.basis: Permitted, sited macro towers provide meaningful physical scarcity and colocation utility, but carriers retain alternative spend paths.

scenarioRobustness.basis: Long contracts and fixed-rate debt improve resilience, but about 93% of first-half site-rental revenue came from three carriers.

substitutionResilience.basis: Macro sites remain important for coverage/capacity, but incremental spend can shift toward small cells, fiber, spectrum efficiency or satellite.

supplyChainResilience.basis: Domestic long-lived physical assets and repaired financing reduce conventional supply exposure, while geographic and carrier-deployment dependence remain.

pricingPower.basis: About five years weighted-average contract term and $22.1B expected future cash inflows support visibility, but concentration and cancellation/default risk constrain pricing power.

riskEvidence.basis: Three-carrier concentration, tenant cancellation/default exposure, reduced diversification and alternative architectures remain material risks.

dataConfidenceEvidence.basis: Recent issuer, SEC, independent industry and current market evidence provide broad coverage; normalized post-DISH leasing growth remains unresolved.

scoreRecord.thesis: Crown Castle is a strategically relevant U.S. macro-tower pure play with scarce physical sites, long contracts and repaired financing, but carrier concentration and churn limit robustness.
scoreRecord.keyRisk: Carrier consolidation, cancellations or capital reallocation away from macro towers can impair leasing growth.
scoreRecord.nextCatalyst: Third-quarter 2026 results and updated tower organic-growth/AFFO outlook.

scoreBreakdown.note: Weighted Methodology 1.0 components, confidence floor multiplier and risk penalty applied conservatively.

items.risk: The divestiture reduces diversification and concentrates exposure in U.S. tower leasing and carrier capital cycles.
Full-year site-rental revenue midpoint remains below 2025 actual, reflecting churn/cancellation pressure despite balance-sheet repair.
Pure-play focus increases exposure to U.S. carrier capital cycles and tenant concentration.
Alternative architectures can shift incremental network spend toward small cells, fiber, satellite or other infrastructure even if macro towers remain necessary.
Carrier/tenant concentration creates discontinuous revenue loss when a major network exits or consolidates.
A pure-play tower portfolio sacrifices fiber/small-cell diversification and makes capital allocation dependent on tower organic growth, debt discipline and shareholder returns.
Cost reductions can improve AFFO but cannot substitute indefinitely for leasing growth.
Tenant concentration can create abrupt revenue and contract-realization losses when a major carrier exits or defaults.
AFFO improvement driven partly by financing and cost relief should not be interpreted as proof that site-rental growth has already normalized.
Approximately 93% of first-half 2026 site-rental revenue came from three national carriers, creating concentrated exposure to their network spending and contract decisions.

items: mobile traffic growth does not guarantee proportional macro-tower leasing growth
carrier capex can shift among macro towers, small cells, fiber, spectrum and satellite architectures
Ericsson is a network-equipment vendor and therefore an industry participant even though it is independent of Crown Castle

contradictions.contradiction: Balance-sheet simplification and debt reduction improve resilience while reported site-rental revenue outlook still implies contraction versus 2025.
Balance-sheet resilience improved sharply after the fiber sale while reported site-rental revenue remains pressured by tenant cancellations.
Debt reduction and cost savings improve AFFO resilience while headline site-rental revenue can still contract because cancellation losses exceed new organic contribution.
Improving AFFO per share coexists with declining site-rental revenue because debt reduction, interest savings and operating efficiencies can offset tenant cancellation pressure.
Long-duration contracts and $22.1 billion of expected future cash inflows improve visibility while counterparty concentration remains structurally high.
Independent network-demand data show strong North American traffic and 5G adoption while Crown Castle's packet records near-term site-rental pressure from tenant cancellations.

unknowns.unknown: Whether pure-play focus produces sustainably higher organic growth after customer churn remains unproven.
Post-sale normalized AFFO growth and reinvestment returns require full council underwriting.
Long-run colocation growth after DISH/Sprint churn and post-sale reinvestment economics remain unproven.
Whether post-cancellation organic growth reaccelerates enough to support durable AFFO growth is not yet established.
The pace at which post-DISH/Sprint organic leasing can offset cancellation losses remains unproven until subsequent operating periods establish sustained net growth.
The degree to which future colocation and amendment growth can diversify economic dependence away from the three largest carriers remains unproven.

unknowns: The evidence does not quantify how much incremental North American traffic will require new Crown Castle macro-tower amendments or colocations.
It does not establish Crown Castle-specific pricing power, valuation, numeric underwriting, or near-term carrier capex allocation.
The precise share of future network densification captured by macro towers versus alternative architectures remains uncertain.
